content: Primary infection with the varicella-zoster virus (commonly known as chickenpox) leads to the virus becoming latent in the dorsal root, cranial, and autonomic ganglia. Reactivation of the virus, often triggered by reduced cellular immunity due to aging, chemotherapy, or immunosuppression, results in herpes zoster (shingles). Shingles typically presents as painful clusters of vesicles on an erythematous base, distributed along one or more dermatomes, and is almost always unilateral, not crossing the midline. In rare cases, the rash can become widespread, involving three or more dermatomes, a condition known as disseminated zoster, which is more common in immunocompromised individuals and can resemble varicella. For all HIV-infected individuals (including pregnant women) with herpes zoster, acyclovir is recommended to prevent disease dissemination and promote resolution at any stage of the disease. Additionally, all individuals presenting with herpes zoster and unknown HIV status should be offered an HIV test, and if positive, assessed for antiretroviral therapy (ART) eligibility. Acyclovir, famciclovir, and valacyclovir are all effective treatments for herpes zoster, with famciclovir and valacyclovir being acceptable alternatives when available. Drug interactions should be considered, particularly with tenofovir, as acyclovir may increase the risk of renal impairment, especially when administered intravenously. Acyclovir is the most accessible and cost-effective option in lowand middle-income countries, though valacyclovir and famciclovir offer simpler dosing regimens. The recommended treatment duration is seven days, or two days after the cessation of new lesion formation. For immunocompromised children, oral acyclovir (80 mg/kg/day in divided doses) or intravenous acyclovir for severe infections is the standard therapy. Adverse effects of these medications are generally mild, including headache and gastrointestinal symptoms. Scabies, caused by the Sarcoptes scabiei mite, is a parasitic skin infection that is particularly problematic in areas with poor sanitation and overcrowding. Transmission occurs through direct skin-to-skin contact, with higher parasite burdens increasing the likelihood of spread. Classic scabies presents with intensely pruritic, erythematous papules and vesicles, often in the interdigital spaces, wrists, axillae, and genital areas. In immunosuppressed individuals, such as those with HIV, atypical presentations, including crusted scabies, are common. Crusted scabies is characterized by hyperkeratotic skin crusts containing large numbers of mites and may involve extensive or atypical areas such as the face and scalp. Diagnosis of scabies is typically clinical, with confirmatory tests including microscopic identification of mites, eggs, or feces. Treatment for mild to moderate scabies in HIV-infected individuals includes topical permethrin 5% or benzyl benzoate, with oral ivermectin recommended for poor treatment response or when topical treatment is not feasible. Severe or crusted scabies requires oral ivermectin (two doses one to two weeks apart) or prolonged topical treatment until clinically clear. Keratolytics, such as 5% salicylic acid, may be used to reduce scale bulk. All household members and close contacts should be treated simultaneously to prevent reinfection, and clothing and bedding should be washed or heat-treated. Molluscum contagiosum, a viral skin infection caused by a poxvirus, is common in children and immunosuppressed individuals, including those with HIV. Lesions are typically pearly white or skin-colored papules with central umbilication and can occur anywhere on the body. In HIV-infected individuals, lesions are often persistent, recurrent, and more severe. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is the primary treatment for extensive or atypical molluscum contagiosum in HIV-infected patients, with no additional specific treatment recommended. New-onset molluscum contagiosum in adults in high HIV-prevalence settings should prompt HIV testing and assessment for ART eligibility. Research gaps remain in the treatment of scabies and molluscum contagiosum, particularly in HIV-infected populations. Future studies should focus on evaluating treatment options for severe forms of these conditions, understanding disease burden, and developing standardized outcome frameworks for comparison across studies.
